## A First‑Day Trade: From Zero to Placing Your First Order Rohit, a recent graduate from Delhi, has saved **₹2 lakh** from his part‑time job. He has read about the **SENSEX** and the **NIFTY 50**, watched news about “the country’s giant” market, and even knows that stocks are traded on an **organized platform** like the BSE and NSE. Yet when he sits down at his laptop, the biggest hurdle is not the market‑price chart or the **price‑discovery** mechanism – it is the practical question: *“How do I actually get my money into the market and buy a share?”* The answer lies in setting up three pieces of infrastructure: 1. **A demat (dematerialised) account** – the electronic vault for your shares. 2. **A trading (broker) account** – the gateway that links you to the exchange. 3. **A trading platform** – the software you will use to place orders, monitor positions, and manage risk. The following sections walk you through each step, from gathering the required documents to pressing “Buy” on your first trade. --- ## 1. Gathering the Documents for KYC and Account Opening In India, **Know‑Your‑Customer (KYC)** regulations are mandatory for any financial service, including opening a demat and trading account. The purpose of KYC is to verify your identity and prevent fraud or money‑laundering. Below is the checklist of documents you will need. | Category | Required Documents (any one of each) | Typical Acceptable Formats | |----------|--------------------------------------|----------------------------| | **Proof of Identity (PoI)** | • PAN Card (mandatory for tax purposes)
• Aadhaar Card
• Passport
• Voter ID | Scanned PDF, JPG, or clear photocopy | | **Proof of Address (PoA)** | • Aadhaar Card (if not used as PoI)
• Utility bill (electricity, water, gas) dated ≤ 3 months ago
• Passport
• Bank statement | Same as above | | **Proof of Income (optional for basic account)** | • Latest Form 16 (if salaried)
• IT‑R filing acknowledgement (ITR‑V)
• Salary slip (last 3 months) | PDF or photocopy | | **Bank Account Details** | • Cancelled cheque or a copy of the first page of your bank passbook showing the account number and IFSC | Clear photocopy | | **Photographs** | • Recent passport‑size colour photograph (white background) | JPEG or scanned image | > **Tip:** Most brokers now allow you to upload these documents through a secure portal on their website or mobile app. Keep the files ready in a folder on your computer or phone to speed up the process. --- ## 2. Completing the KYC Process and Opening a Demat Account ### 2.1. Choose a Depository Participant (DP) A **Depository Participant (DP)** is the intermediary that holds your securities in the **dematerialised (demat) system**. In India, the two main depositories are **National Securities Depository Limited (NSDL)** and **Central Depository Services Limited (CDSL)**. Almost every broker is a DP, but you can also open a demat account directly with a DP if you prefer (e.g., through a bank that offers demat services). **For beginners, the simplest route** is to open a **combined demat‑plus‑trading account** with a broker who is also a DP. This eliminates the need for a separate account and reduces paperwork. ### 2.2. Step‑by‑Step Online KYC 1. **Visit the broker’s website or download its mobile app.** 2. **Select “Open New Account”** → “Demat & Trading Account.” 3. **Enter your basic details:** name, mobile number, email, date of birth, PAN. 4. **Upload the KYC documents** from the checklist above. 5. **Complete the e‑KYC verification:** - **Aadhaar OTP** – you will receive a one‑time password on your registered mobile number. - **Video KYC (if required)** – a short 2‑minute video where you show your ID and answer a few questions. 6. **Sign the agreement electronically** (e‑sign) using your Aadhaar‑linked DigiLocker or a digital signature certificate. 7. **Set up your login credentials** – user ID, password, and a transaction password (used for order placement). 8. **Fund your trading account** – transfer money from your linked bank account to the broker’s client‑segregated account (usually via NEFT/RTGS or UPI). After the broker’s compliance team reviews the documents (typically 1‑3 business days), you will receive a **DP ID** (e.g., **IN123456**) and a **Client ID**. These numbers are your unique identifiers for all future transactions. > **What if you already have a demat account?** > You can **link** your existing demat account to a new broker’s trading account, provided the broker supports “demat‑linking.” This avoids opening a second demat account and saves on annual maintenance charges. --- ## 3. Choosing the Right Broker A broker is the bridge between you and the exchange. Selecting one involves balancing three core criteria: **fees**, **reliability**, and **features**. ### 3.1. Fee Structure | Fee Type | What It Covers | Typical Range for Beginners* | |----------|----------------|------------------------------| | **Brokerage (per trade)** | Charge on each buy/sell order (percentage of turnover) | 0.01 % – 0.05 % (often capped at ₹20 – ₹50) | | **Account‑keeping/Annual Maintenance Charge (AMC)** | Custody cost for the demat account | ₹300 – ₹500 per year (some brokers waive for the first year) | | **Transaction Charges** | Exchange levy (BSE/NSE), GST, SEBI turnover fee | Fixed by the exchange; passed through to you | | **Other Charges** | Call‑and‑trade, margin usage, data feed | Varies; usually minimal for a basic plan | \*Numbers are indicative as of 2026; always verify the latest tariff on the broker’s website. **Cheapest‑only** is not always the best choice. Extremely low brokerage may come with limited research tools or poorer customer support. ### 3.2. Reliability - **Regulatory status:** Must be a **registered broker** with SEBI and a member of either BSE, NSE, or both. - **Technology uptime:** Look for brokers that publish **system‑availability statistics** (e.g., 99.9 % uptime). - **Customer support:** 24 × 7 phone, chat, and email; preferably with a local office in major cities. ### 3.3. Features | Feature | Why It Matters for a Beginner | |---------|--------------------------------| | **Intuitive UI** | Reduces learning curve; you can find “Buy”/“Sell” buttons quickly. | | **Educational resources** | In‑app tutorials, webinars, and mock‑trading (paper‑trading) accounts. | | **Research & analysis** | Access to company reports, analyst ratings, and market news. | | **Mobile app quality** | Ability to trade on the go; push notifications for order status. | | **Advanced order types** | Support for stop‑loss, cover‑order, bracket‑order, etc. | ### 3.4. Popular Brokers for Indian Beginners (as of 2026) | Broker | Brokerage (Equity) | AMC | Notable Features | |--------|-------------------|-----|------------------| | **Zerodha** | 0.01 % (min ₹20) | ₹300 (first year free) | Kite web & mobile app, extensive tutorials, low fees | | **Upstox** | 0.05 % (min ₹20) | ₹250 (first year free) | Fast order execution, integrated charting | | **Angel One** | 0.01 % (min ₹20) | ₹300 | Research hub, “Angel Research” reports | | **ICICI Direct** | 0.5 % (min ₹20) | ₹600 | Full‑service brokerage, banking integration | | **HDFC Securities** | 0.5 % (min ₹20) | ₹550 | Strong customer service, wide branch network | > **Choosing tip:** Start with a **discount broker** (Zerodha, Upstox, Angel One) if you prefer low costs and are comfortable learning on your own. Switch to a full‑service broker later if you need personalised advisory. --- ## 4. Navigating a Typical Trading Platform Once your account is live and funded, you will interact with the broker’s **trading platform**. Most brokers provide both a **web‑based interface** and a **mobile app**. The layout is largely similar across platforms, and the core elements are: 1. **Watchlist / Market Screener** – List of stocks you are interested in, with live price, change %, and volume. 2. **Quote Window** – Detailed view of a selected stock, showing bid/ask, market depth, and key statistics (e.g., P/E ratio, dividend yield). 3. **Order Entry Box** – Where you specify **Buy** or **Sell**, quantity, and order type. 4. **Position Book** – Summary of your current holdings, average cost, unrealised P/L. 5. **Order Book** – List of pending (open) orders and their status (filled, partially filled, cancelled). 6. **Funds/Balance Section** – Shows cash available for trading, margin utilised, and total equity. ### 4.1. Walk‑through: Placing a Simple Market Order 1. **Log in** using your user ID, password, and transaction password. 2. **Search** for the ticker symbol (e.g., “RELIANCE”) in the **Watchlist** or **Search Bar**. 3. Click the **Buy** button next to the ticker. 4. In the **Order Entry Box**, select **“Market”** as the order type. 5. Enter the **quantity** (e.g., 10 shares). 6. Review the **estimated cost** (share price × quantity + brokerage). 7. Click **“Place Order.”** The order is routed instantly to the exchange and should be filled at the prevailing market price. ### 4.2. Visual Cues to Avoid Mistakes - **Red “Sell” button** vs. **Green “Buy” button** – colour coding helps prevent accidental opposite‑side trades. - **Confirmation pop‑up** – always double‑check the ticker, quantity, and order type before confirming. - **Order status icons** – a green check means filled; a yellow hourglass indicates pending; a red cross means rejected (often due to insufficient funds or price limits). --- ## 5. Understanding Order Types Choosing the right order type is essential for controlling execution price and managing risk. Below are the most common order types you will encounter on Indian trading platforms. ### 5.1. Market Order - **Definition:** Executes immediately at the best available price in the market. - **When to use:** When you want to guarantee execution (e.g., buying a highly liquid stock) and are less concerned about the exact price. - **Risk:** In fast‑moving markets, the fill price may differ from the last‑quoted price (slippage). ### 5.2. Limit Order - **Definition:** Sets a **price ceiling** (for buying) or **price floor** (for selling). The order will only execute at that price **or better**. - **When to use:** When you have a target entry or exit price and are willing to wait. - **Example:** Want to buy **TCS** at ₹3,200 or less → place a **Buy Limit** at ₹3,200. If the market never reaches this level, the order remains unfilled. ### 5.3. Stop‑Loss (SL) Order - **Definition:** Becomes a market order once the stock reaches a predefined **trigger price** (the “stop”). - **Purpose:** To limit downside risk by exiting a position automatically if the price moves unfavourably. - **Example:** You own **HDFC Bank** bought at ₹1,700. Set a **Stop‑Loss** at ₹1,620. If the price falls to ₹1,620, the order triggers and sells at the next available market price. ### 5.4. Stop‑Limit Order (Advanced) - **Definition:** Combines a stop‑loss trigger with a limit price. Once the stop price is hit, a **limit order** is placed instead of a market order. - **When to use:** When you want to avoid the potential price gap of a plain stop‑loss but still want an automatic exit. - **Caution:** If the market moves past your limit price quickly, the order may remain unfilled, exposing you to greater loss. ### 5.5. Bracket Order (BO) – A Built‑In Risk Management Tool Many platforms (especially for intraday trading) offer a **Bracket Order** that bundles three legs: 1. **Entry order** (market or limit). 2. **Target order** – a limit order to take profit at a pre‑defined price. 3. **Stop‑loss order** – a market order that triggers if the price moves against you. The BO automatically cancels the opposite leg once either the target or stop‑loss is hit, ensuring you are never in the market twice. --- ## 6. Putting It All Together: Rohit’s First Trade 1. **Documents ready:** Rohit scans his PAN, Aadhaar, and a recent electricity bill. 2. **Broker selection:** He chooses **Zerodha** for its low brokerage and intuitive **Kite** platform. 3. **Account opening:** He completes the e‑KYC in 15 minutes, uploads the documents, and funds his account with **₹2 lakh** via UPI. 4. **Platform navigation:** After logging into Kite, he adds **RELIANCE**, **TCS**, and **HDFC Bank** to his watchlist. 5. **Order decision:** Rohit wants to buy 5 shares of **RELIANCE** at the current market price, but he also wants to protect against a sudden drop. He places a **Buy Market** order for 5 shares and simultaneously sets a **Stop‑Loss** at ₹2,250 (current price ₹2,320). 6. **Execution:** The market order fills instantly at ₹2,322 per share. The stop‑loss order is now pending at ₹2,250. If the price falls to that level, the stop‑loss will trigger a market sell, limiting his loss. Within a single session, Rohit has moved from a savings account to owning a real share, with a risk‑management guard in place. --- ## 7. Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them | Pitfall | Why It Happens | Preventive Action | |---------|----------------|-------------------| | **Using the wrong order type** (e.g., market instead of limit) | Inexperience with price volatility | Always double‑check the selected order type before confirming. | | **Insufficient funds for brokerage** | Forgetting that brokerage is deducted from cash balance | Keep a small buffer (₹1,000 – ₹2,000) in your trading account to cover fees. | | **Leaving a stop‑loss too tight** | Fear of loss leads to premature exit | Set stop‑loss based on technical support levels or a percentage (e.g., 3‑5 % below entry). | | **Ignoring platform notifications** | Disabling push alerts or not checking order status | Enable real‑time notifications for order fills, rejections, and margin calls. | | **Opening multiple demat accounts** | Believing more accounts give more flexibility | Remember that each additional demat account incurs extra AMC; a single account is sufficient for most beginners. | --- ## 8. Next Steps After the Setup - **Practice with a virtual account** (paper‑trading) if your broker offers one. - **Review your first trade**: note the execution price, brokerage paid, and any slippage. - **Start building a watchlist** of stocks that align with the **investment strategies** you learned earlier. - **Read the company’s financial statements** (refer to the earlier chapter) before adding a stock to your portfolio. These actions will reinforce the infrastructure you have just built and transition you from a passive observer to an active market participant. --- ## Key Takeaways - **KYC compliance** requires a PAN, proof of identity, proof of address, bank details, and a photo; upload them through the broker’s portal. - **Demat account** creation is most straightforward when combined with a trading account at a broker who is also a DP. - **Broker selection** balances low fees, regulatory reliability, and platform features; discount brokers like Zerodha, Upstox, and Angel One are popular among beginners. - **Typical trading platforms** consist of a watchlist, quote window, order entry box, position book, order book, and funds section; mastering these screens enables efficient order placement. - **Order types**: - *Market* – immediate execution, possible slippage. - *Limit* – execution only at a specified price or better. - *Stop‑Loss* – market order triggered at a price to limit loss. - *Stop‑Limit* – limit order triggered at a price, protecting against extreme gaps. - *Bracket* – combines entry, target, and stop‑loss for automated risk management. - **Practical tip**: Always verify the order type, quantity, and price before confirming, and keep a modest cash buffer for brokerage and transaction charges. With your demat and trading accounts live, a reliable broker chosen, and a clear understanding of the platform and order mechanics, you are now equipped to move from theory to practice and begin building your investment portfolio. Happy trading!

modules.title: Fundamental Analysis: Evaluating Companies
modules.content:
## A Real‑World Decision: Ravi’s Dilemma Ravi, a software engineer from Bengaluru, has saved **₹2 lakh** from his first few years of work. He has already opened a demat account and knows how to place an order on the NSE Trade‑Now platform. The next step for him is to decide **which share to buy**. Two names keep popping up in his research: | Company | Sector | Current Price (₹) | 5‑Year Revenue CAGR | |---------|--------|-------------------|----------------------| | **Alpha Textiles Ltd.** | Textiles | 185 | 12 % | | **Beta Power Corp.** | Power Generation | 412 | 8 % | Both stocks have shown price appreciation, but Ravi is unsure which one truly offers a better **long‑term growth prospect**. He wants to move beyond headlines and use a systematic, numbers‑driven approach. The tools he needs are exactly what this chapter will teach: **ratio analysis, management assessment, industry evaluation, a simple discounted cash flow (DCF) calculation, and a screening checklist**. By the end of the chapter, Ravi (and you) will be able to answer questions like: - *Is the company profitable enough to sustain growth?* - *Does the management have a track record of creating shareholder value?* - *How does the industry outlook affect the company’s future?* - *What is the intrinsic value of the share, and is it trading at a discount?* --- ## 1. Ratio Analysis – The First Lens Financial ratios condense the information from the income statement, balance sheet, and cash‑flow statement into bite‑size indicators. For a beginner, focus on three families of ratios: 1. **Profitability Ratios** – How efficiently does the business turn sales into profit? 2. **Valuation Ratios** – How expensive is the stock relative to its earnings or cash flow? 3. **Efficiency & Solvency Ratios** – How well does the company use its assets and manage debt? Below, each ratio is introduced with a simple formula, a brief interpretation, and a **quick example** using the two companies from Ravi’s list. (All figures are illustrative.) ### 1.1 Profitability Ratios | Ratio | Formula | What It Tells You | Example | |-------|---------|-------------------|---------| | **Net Profit Margin** | Net Income ÷ Revenue | Portion of each rupee of sales that remains as profit. Higher = better cost control. | Alpha: ₹150 cr ÷ ₹12,000 cr = **1.25 %**.
Beta: ₹420 cr ÷ ₹30,000 cr = **1.40 %**. | | **Return on Equity (ROE)** | Net Income ÷ Shareholders’ Equity | How much profit is generated per rupee of equity. Indicates management’s ability to use capital. | Alpha: ₹150 cr ÷ ₹9,000 cr = **1.67 %**.
Beta: ₹420 cr ÷ ₹25,000 cr = **1.68 %**. | | **Return on Capital Employed (ROCE)** | EBIT ÷ (Total Assets – Current Liabilities) | Efficiency of capital use, independent of financing mix. | Alpha: ₹210 cr ÷ (₹15,000 cr – ₹5,000 cr) = **2.10 %**.
Beta: ₹600 cr ÷ (₹35,000 cr – ₹8,000 cr) = **2.18 %**. | > **Tip for beginners:** Compare each ratio to the **industry average** (available on NSE or financial portals). A company that beats its peers on profitability is often a safer bet. ### 1.2 Valuation Ratios | Ratio | Formula | What It Tells You | Example | |-------|---------|-------------------|---------| | **Price‑Earnings (P/E) Ratio** | Market Price per Share ÷ Earnings per Share (EPS) | How many rupees investors are willing to pay for each rupee of earnings. Lower may indicate undervaluation, but watch for growth expectations. | Alpha: ₹185 ÷ ₹7 = **26.4×**.
Beta: ₹412 ÷ ₹25 = **16.5×**. | | **Price‑Book (P/B) Ratio** | Market Price per Share ÷ Book Value per Share | Relates market price to net asset value. Useful for asset‑heavy sectors like textiles. | Alpha: ₹185 ÷ ₹120 = **1.54×**.
Beta: ₹412 ÷ ₹250 = **1.65×**. | | **EV/EBITDA** (Enterprise Value ÷ EBITDA) | (Market Cap + Debt – Cash) ÷ EBITDA | Captures total firm value relative to operating cash flow. Lower multiples often signal cheaper valuation. | Alpha: ₹22 bn ÷ ₹300 cr = **7.3×**.
Beta: ₹55 bn ÷ ₹900 cr = **6.1×**. | > **Caution:** A low P/E may be tempting, but it can also signal declining earnings. Always cross‑check with profitability trends. ### 1.3 Efficiency & Solvency Ratios | Ratio | Formula | Insight | Example | |-------|---------|---------|---------| | **Debt‑to‑Equity (D/E)** | Total Debt ÷ Shareholders’ Equity | Higher debt increases financial risk. | Alpha: ₹4,500 cr ÷ ₹9,000 cr = **0.5×**.
Beta: ₹10,000 cr ÷ ₹25,000 cr = **0.4×**. | | **Current Ratio** | Current Assets ÷ Current Liabilities | Short‑term liquidity cushion. Ratio > 1 is generally comfortable. | Alpha: ₹6,000 cr ÷ ₹4,000 cr = **1.5×**.
Beta: ₹12,000 cr ÷ ₹9,000 cr = **1.33×**. | | **Asset Turnover** | Revenue ÷ Total Assets | How many rupees of sales are generated per rupee of assets. Higher indicates efficient use of assets. | Alpha: ₹12,000 cr ÷ ₹15,000 cr = **0.80×**.
Beta: ₹30,000 cr ÷ ₹35,000 cr = **0.86×**. | **Takeaway:** By scanning these ratios, Ravi can quickly spot which company is more profitable, cheaper, and financially sound relative to its peers. --- ## 2. Management Quality & Corporate Governance Numbers tell the story, but **who is writing the script** matters equally. Good management can navigate a company through industry cycles, while weak governance can erode shareholder value. ### 2.1 What to Look For - **Track Record:** Has the CEO delivered on past growth targets? Look for consistent earnings growth over 3‑5 years. - **Ownership Alignment:** Do promoters or insiders hold a significant stake (> 20 %)? Higher skin‑in‑the‑game often aligns interests. - **Board Composition:** Independent directors, gender diversity, and expertise relevant to the business. - **Audit Quality:** Is the auditor a reputable firm (e.g., Big Four)? Frequent changes in auditors may raise red flags. - **Shareholder Rights:** Existence of a **shareholder‑friendly policy**—e.g., regular dividend payouts, right to vote, and transparent communication. ### 2.2 Sources of Information - **Annual Reports** (refer back to the “Financial Fundamentals” chapter for where to find them). - **Corporate Governance Scores** published by the NSE or SEBI’s “Corporate Governance Index”. - **Management Discussion & Analysis (MD&A)** section – reads like a letter from the CEO; watch for vague statements versus concrete plans. - **News & Regulatory Filings** – any recent penalties, related‑party transactions, or insider trading disclosures. ### 2.3 Red Flags for Beginners | Red Flag | Why It Matters | |----------|----------------| | **Frequent CEO turnover** (more than once in 3 years) | May indicate strategic disagreements or performance issues. | | **High related‑party transactions** without clear justification | Can hide profit shifting or asset misallocation. | | **Low promoter holding (< 5 %)** in a family‑run business | Might suggest lack of confidence or potential takeover risk. | | **Negative audit opinions** | Signals concerns about financial reporting reliability. | Applying this checklist, Ravi discovers that **Alpha Textiles** has a promoter holding of 28 % and a stable CEO tenure of 7 years, while **Beta Power** has a relatively low promoter stake (12 %) and a CEO who changed hands two years ago. This tilts the qualitative balance slightly toward Alpha, despite Beta’s marginally lower valuation multiples. --- ## 3. Industry Trends & Competitive Positioning Even a stellar company can falter if its industry is in decline. Conversely, a modest firm in a booming sector may deliver robust returns. ### 3.1 Mapping the Industry Life Cycle 1. **Emergence** – High growth, low competition, high margins. 2. **Growth** – Rapid revenue expansion, entry of new players. 3. **Maturity** – Saturation, margin pressure, focus on efficiency. 4. **Decline** – Shrinking demand, excess capacity. Identify where the company’s sector sits on this curve. For **textiles**, India is still in a **growth** phase, driven by rising domestic consumption and export demand. **Power generation** is largely **mature**, with regulatory caps on tariffs and a shift toward renewable sources. ### 3.2 Porter’s Five Forces – A Quick Scan | Force | Question to Ask | Typical Impact in India | |-------|-----------------|--------------------------| | **Threat of New Entrants** | Are barriers (capital, regulation) high? | Power sector: high (license, capital). Textiles: moderate (machinery cost, brand). | | **Bargaining Power of Suppliers** | Dependence on raw material (cotton, coal). | Textiles face volatile cotton prices; Power relies on fuel contracts. | | **Bargaining Power of Buyers** | Concentration of buyers, price sensitivity. | Textiles: fragmented retailers, price‑sensitive. Power: large utilities, regulated tariffs. | | **Threat of Substitutes** | Availability of alternative products. | Textiles: synthetic fabrics compete. Power: renewable energy is a growing substitute. | | **Rivalry Among Existing Competitors** | Number of players, capacity utilisation. | Both sectors have intense competition, but power has higher consolidation. | A sector with **low threat of substitutes** and **high barriers to entry** generally offers a stronger **economic moat**—a durable competitive advantage. ### 3.3 Competitive Moats in the Indian Context - **Cost Advantage:** Ability to produce at lower cost (e.g., economies of scale, low‑cost labor). - **Brand Loyalty:** Recognizable consumer brands (e.g., textiles with a heritage label). - **Regulatory Licences:** Power plants with long‑term PPAs (Power Purchase Agreements). - **Network Effects:** Distribution networks that are hard to replicate. Ravi notes that **Alpha Textiles** owns a well‑known heritage brand and operates several captive cotton farms, giving it a **cost advantage**. **Beta Power** holds a mix of coal‑based and renewable assets, but its newer renewable plants are still under construction, exposing it to **execution risk**. --- ## 4. Estimating Intrinsic Value – A Simple DCF Walk‑Through The **discounted cash flow (DCF)** method estimates the present value of a company’s future cash flows. For beginners, a **two‑step** approach works well: 1. **Project Free Cash Flow (FCF)** for the next 5 years. 2. **Calculate Terminal Value** and discount everything back using a reasonable **cost of capital** (WACC). ### 4.1 Step‑by‑Step DCF for a Mid‑Cap Indian Company Assume Ravi wants to evaluate **Alpha Textiles**. | Year | Revenue (₹ cr) | Growth Rate | EBIT (₹ cr) | Tax (30 %) | NOPAT (₹ cr) | Depreciation (₹ cr) | Capital Expenditure (₹ cr) | Change in Working Capital (₹ cr) | **FCF** (₹ cr) | |------|----------------|------------|------------|------------|--------------|---------------------|----------------------------|-----------------------------------|----------------| | 2024 | 12,000 | 12 % | 210 | 63 | 147 | 30 | 40 | 5 | **132** | | 2025 | 13,440 | 12 % | 235 | 70.5 | 164.5 | 32 | 42 | 5.5 | **149** | | 2026 | 15,053 | 12 % | 263 | 78.9 | 184.1 | 34 | 44 | 6 | **168** | | 2027 | 16,860 | 12 % | 295 | 88.5 | 206.5 | 36 | 46 | 6.5 | **190** | | 2028 | 18,883 | 12 % | 332 | 99.6 | 232.4 | 38 | 48 | 7 | **215** | *Simplifications*: Use a constant tax rate, assume depreciation grows with revenue, and keep capital expenditure and working‑capital changes roughly in line with growth. #### 4.2 Terminal Value Assume a **stable growth rate** of 5 % after 2028 (reflecting long‑term GDP growth). Terminal Value = **FCF₍2028₎ × (1 + g) ÷ (WACC − g)** Pick a **Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC)** of **10 %** (typical for Indian mid‑caps). Terminal Value = 215 cr × 1.05 ÷ (0.10 − 0.05) = **₹4,515 cr**. #### 4.3 Discounting Discount each year’s FCF and the terminal value back to present value (PV) using the formula **PV = Cash Flow ÷ (1 + WACC)ᵗ**. | Year | Discount Factor (10 %) | PV of FCF (₹ cr) | |------|------------------------|-------------------| | 2024 | 0.909 | 120 | | 2025 | 0.826 | 123 | | 2026 | 0.751 | 126 | | 2027 | 0.683 | 130 | | 2028 | 0.621 | 133 | | Terminal (2028) | 0.621 | 2,804 | **Enterprise Value (EV) = Σ PV of FCF + PV of Terminal = ₹3,436 cr**. #### 4.4 From EV to Intrinsic Share Price 1. **Subtract Net Debt** (Debt − Cash). Suppose Alpha has **₹4,500 cr debt** and **₹1,200 cr cash** → Net Debt = **₹3,300 cr**. 2. **Equity Value = EV − Net Debt = ₹3,436 cr − ₹3,300 cr = ₹136 cr**. 3. **Shares Outstanding** = 7 cr. 4. **Intrinsic Price per Share = ₹136 cr ÷ 7 cr = ₹19.4**. The current market price is **₹185**, far above the intrinsic estimate. This suggests the stock may be **overvalued** unless growth expectations are higher than our modest 12 % projection. > **Lesson for beginners:** Even a simple DCF can highlight a large gap between market price and intrinsic value, prompting a deeper look at assumptions. --- ## 5. Screening & Shortlisting Stocks – A Practical Checklist Ravi now wants to **filter the universe of Indian listed companies** to a manageable list before diving deeper. A systematic screen saves time and keeps the analysis objective. ### 5.1 Core Screening Criteria | Criterion | Reason | Typical Threshold (for Indian equities) | |-----------|--------|------------------------------------------| | **Market Capitalisation** | Ensures sufficient liquidity and analyst coverage. | > ₹5 billion (mid‑cap and above). | | **P/E Ratio** | Avoids extremely over‑priced stocks. | < 25× (adjust for sector norms). | | **ROE** | Captures efficient capital use. | > 10 %. | | **Debt‑to‑Equity** | Limits financial risk. | < 0.6×. | | **Revenue Growth (3 yr CAGR)** | Indicates momentum. | > 8 %. | | **Dividend Yield** (optional) | For investors seeking cash flow. | > 2 % (if dividend‑oriented). | | **Corporate Governance Score** | Aligns with shareholder interests. | ≥ 8/10 (NSE rating). | ### 5.2 Using Free Tools 1. **NSE India website** – Under “Equity > Screener”, input the above thresholds. 2. **Moneycontrol.com** – Offers advanced filters and industry‑wise lists. 3. **Yahoo Finance (India)** – Quick snapshot of key ratios. Export the filtered list to Excel, then **rank** companies by a composite score (e.g., weighted sum of ROE, revenue growth, and governance). Ravi’s final shortlist might look like: | Rank | Company | Sector | P/E | ROE | D/E | 3‑yr Rev CAGR | |------|---------|--------|-----|-----|-----|----------------| | 1 | Alpha Textiles Ltd. | Textiles | 26.4 | 1.67 % | 0.5 | 12 % | | 2 | Gamma Pharma Ltd. | Pharmaceuticals | 22.1 | 12 % | 0.3 | 15 % | | 3 | Delta Infra Ltd. | Infrastructure | 18.9 | 9 % | 0.4 | 9 % | *(Numbers are illustrative; actual data will differ.)* ### 5​.3 From List to Deep Dive Pick the **top 2–3** stocks from the shortlist and perform the full analysis covered in Sections 1‑4: ratio deep‑dive, management check, industry outlook, and a DCF valuation. The stock that scores best across **both quantitative and qualitative dimensions** becomes Ravi’s **candidate for purchase**. --- ## 6. Putting It All Together – A Mini‑Case Study ### 6.1 The Choice Ravi runs the numbers for **Alpha Textiles** (intrinsic price ₹19.4) and **Beta Power** (using a similar DCF, intrinsic price ₹380). The market prices are **₹185** and **₹412**, respectively. Both appear overvalued, but Beta Power’s premium is **smaller** (≈ 8 % over intrinsic) versus Alpha’s **nearly 10×** premium. ### 6.2 Qualitative Edge - **Management:** Alpha’s stable leadership and strong promoter stake provide confidence. - **Industry:** Textiles are in a growth phase with rising domestic demand, while power is mature and facing regulatory pressure. - **Moat:** Alpha’s captive cotton farms and heritage brand give a modest cost advantage; Beta’s reliance on coal may erode margins as renewable policies tighten. ### 6.3 Decision Balancing the **higher valuation discount** of Beta Power against the **stronger qualitative factors** of Alpha Textiles, Ravi decides to **wait for a price correction** in Alpha (perhaps a pull‑back to ₹120–₹130) before entering. Meanwhile, he keeps Beta Power on his watchlist, ready to buy if the market dips below ₹380. > **Key lesson:** Fundamental analysis is not about finding a “perfect” stock, but about **understanding trade‑offs** and aligning them with your investment horizon and risk tolerance. --- ## Key Takeaways - **Ratio analysis** provides a quick health check: profitability (Net Profit Margin, ROE, ROCE), valuation (P/E, P/B, EV/EBITDA), and efficiency/solvency (D/E, Current Ratio, Asset Turnover). - **Management quality** and corporate governance are assessed through tenure, ownership alignment, board independence, audit credibility, and shareholder‑rights policies. - **Industry dynamics**—life‑cycle stage, Porter’s Five Forces, and competitive moats—shape a company’s long‑term growth prospects. - A **basic DCF** (projecting free cash flow for 5 years, adding a terminal value, and discounting at a realistic WACC) yields an intrinsic share price that can be compared with the market price. - **Screening** with clear quantitative thresholds (market cap, P/E, ROE, D/E, revenue growth, governance score) narrows the universe to a shortlist, enabling deeper qualitative analysis. - The final investment decision balances **valuation gaps**, **management credibility**, and **industry outlook**, as illustrated by Ravi’s case study. By mastering these steps, a beginner investor can move from **guesswork** to a **structured, evidence‑based** approach to selecting Indian equities that align with personal financial goals.

modules.content:
## A Real‑World Decision: When to Buy a Stock After a Sharp Drop

Rohit, a first‑time investor in Mumbai, has been watching the **Reliance Industries Ltd. (RIL)** share price on his BSE Online dashboard. Over the past two weeks the stock slipped from ₹2,500 to ₹2,200 – a 12 % decline that made his friends warn, “It’s a bad time to buy.” Yet Rohit remembers a line from the earlier chapter *Investment Strategies for Beginners*: “Market dips can present buying opportunities if the underlying fundamentals remain strong.”  
He now wonders:

- **Is the price drop a temporary pull‑back or the start of a new downtrend?**  
- **Can the chart tell him whether the price might bounce back soon?**  

The tools of **technical analysis** – candlestick patterns, support‑resistance zones, moving averages, and momentum indicators – are designed to answer exactly these questions. The sections that follow unpack each tool, show how to read them on a chart, and then walk Rohit (and you) through a concrete analysis of RIL’s recent price action.

---

## 1. Reading Candlestick Charts

### 1.1 What a Candlestick Shows

A **candlestick** is a visual summary of price activity for a chosen time‑frame (e.g., one day, one hour). Each candle consists of:

| Part | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| **Body** | The rectangle between the **open** and **close** prices. A **green (or white)** body means the close > open (price rose). A **red (or black)** body means the close < open (price fell). |
| **Wicks (or shadows)** | Thin lines extending above and below the body. The upper wick shows the **high** of the period; the lower wick shows the **low**. |
| **Real‑body length** | Indicates the strength of the move. A long body signals strong buying or selling pressure; a short body suggests indecision. |

Because the Indian market operates on an **organized platform** with transparent price discovery, each daily candle on the BSE chart reflects the collective actions of thousands of traders – a snapshot of market sentiment for that day.

### 1.2 Common Single‑Candle Patterns

| Pattern | Visual Cue | Typical Interpretation |
|---------|------------|------------------------|
| **Marubozu** | No wicks; long body | Very strong buying (green) or selling (red) pressure. |
| **Doji** | Small body; wicks of similar length | Indecision; possible reversal when followed by a confirming candle. |
| **Hammer** (green) / **Hanging Man** (red) | Small body, long lower wick, little upper wick | Bullish reversal (hammer) after a downtrend; bearish reversal (hanging man) after an uptrend. |

### 1.3 Multi‑Candle Patterns for Entry/Exit Signals

| Pattern | Composition | Signal |
|---------|-------------|--------|
| **Bullish Engulfing** | A small red candle followed by a larger green candle that completely engulfs it. | Potential start of an upward move. |
| **Bearish Engulfing** | Opposite of bullish. | Potential start of a downward move. |
| **Morning Star** | Three‑candle formation: long red, short (doji or small body), long green. | Strong bullish reversal. |
| **Evening Star** | Mirror image of the Morning Star. | Strong bearish reversal. |

**Practical tip:** When a pattern appears near a known **support** or **resistance** level (covered next), its predictive power increases.

---

## 2. Support and Resistance Levels

### 2.1 Defining the Zones

- **Support** – a price level where buying interest historically outweighs selling, causing the price to **pause or bounce upward**. Think of it as a floor under the price.
- **Resistance** – a price level where selling interest historically outweighs buying, causing the price to **stall or fall**. Think of it as a ceiling.

These zones emerge from the **price discovery** process discussed earlier: as traders place orders, clusters of buy or sell orders form at certain price points, creating invisible “walls” on the chart.

### 2.2 How to Spot Support/Resistance

1. **Visual inspection** – Look for multiple peaks (resistance) or troughs (support) where the price has reversed in the past.
2. **Horizontal lines** – Draw a line connecting at least two high points (resistance) or two low points (support). The more touches, the stronger the level.
3. **Round numbers** – In Indian markets, levels ending in “00” or “50” (e.g., ₹2,250) often act as psychological support/resistance.

### 2.3 Role in Trade Management

- **Entry point** – Buying near support (especially after a bullish candlestick) can improve risk‑reward.
- **Exit point** – Setting a **profit target** just below a resistance level helps lock in gains.
- **Stop‑loss** – Placing a stop just below support (for a long trade) limits downside if the support fails.

### 2.4 Example: RIL’s Recent Support

On the daily BSE chart, RIL fell to **₹2,210** on 15 May, bounced to **₹2,260** on 17 May, and then retreated again. The **₹2,200–₹2,220** band has been tested three times in the last month, making it a **strong support zone**. A bullish candlestick forming inside this band could be a green light for a long entry.

---

## 3. Moving Averages: Smoothing the Noise

### 3.1 What Is a Moving Average?

A **moving average (MA)** is the arithmetic mean of a security’s price over a set number of periods, recalculated each period. It smooths out short‑term fluctuations, revealing the underlying trend.

- **Simple Moving Average (SMA)** – Adds up closing prices for *N* periods and divides by *N*.
- **Exponential Moving Average (EMA)** – Gives more weight to recent prices, reacting faster to changes.

### 3.2 Common Periods for Indian Stocks

| Period | Typical Use |
|--------|-------------|
| **20‑day SMA** | Short‑term trend; aligns with roughly one month of trading days. |
| **50‑day SMA** | Intermediate trend; often used to gauge medium‑term direction. |
| **200‑day SMA** | Long‑term trend; acts as a “market health” barometer. |

### 3.3 How to Use Moving Averages

1. **Trend Direction**  
   - If the price is **above** the MA, the market is generally **bullish**.  
   - If the price is **below** the MA, the market is generally **bearish**.

2. **Crossovers** – When a **short‑term MA** (e.g., 20‑day) crosses **above** a **long‑term MA** (e.g., 50‑day), it creates a **golden cross**, signaling potential upward momentum. The opposite, a **death cross**, may warn of a downtrend.

3. **Dynamic Support/Resistance** – Prices often respect the MA as a moving support (in an uptrend) or resistance (in a downtrend).

### 3.4 Applying MAs to the Sample Stock

On RIL’s chart:

- The **20‑day SMA** sits at **₹2,250**.  
- The price on 20 May closed at **₹2,260**, just **above** the SMA – a bullish sign.  
- The **50‑day SMA** is at **₹2,300**. Since the price is still **below** the 50‑day SMA, the longer‑term trend remains **neutral to slightly bearish**.  

A **golden cross** would occur if the 20‑day SMA moves above the 50‑day SMA, which could be a stronger entry signal.

---

## 4. Momentum Indicators: RSI and MACD

### 4.1 Relative Strength Index (RSI)

- **Formula**: RSI = 100 – [100 / (1 + RS)], where **RS** is the average gain divided by the average loss over a chosen period (commonly 14 days).  
- **Scale**: 0 – 100.  
- **Interpretation**  
  - **Above 70** – The stock may be **overbought**; a pull‑back could be imminent.  
  - **Below 30** – The stock may be **oversold**; a bounce could be likely.  
  - **Crossing the 50‑line** – Indicates a shift in momentum.

**Why it matters for Rohit:** After RIL’s dip to ₹2,200, the 14‑day RSI fell to **28**, signaling oversold conditions. This aligns with the support zone, reinforcing the potential for a rebound.

### 4.2 Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD)

- **Components**  
  - **MACD Line** = 12‑day EMA – 26‑day EMA.  
  - **Signal Line** = 9‑day EMA of the MACD Line.  
  - **Histogram** = MACD Line – Signal Line (visualizes the distance between the two).

- **Key Signals**  
  - **Bullish crossover** – MACD Line moves **above** the Signal Line → possible uptrend.  
  - **Bearish crossover** – MACD Line moves **below** the Signal Line → possible downtrend.  
  - **Histogram turning positive** – Momentum shifting upward.

**Applying MACD to RIL:**  
On 18 May, the MACD histogram turned from negative to positive while the MACD Line crossed above the Signal Line. This bullish divergence coincided with a green candlestick near support, adding confidence to a long entry.

### 4.3 Combining RSI and MACD

When **both** indicators suggest a reversal (RSI < 30 **and** MACD bullish crossover), the probability of a true turnaround improves. This “double‑confirmation” approach is a simple yet powerful filter for beginners.

---

## 5. Putting It All Together: A Step‑by‑Step Trend Analysis

Below is a concise workflow that Rohit (and any new investor) can follow on the BSE Online platform or any charting tool that provides candlesticks, moving averages, and indicators.

### 5.1 The Workflow

1. **Select the Time‑Frame** – For a medium‑term view, start with the **daily chart**.  
2. **Identify Support/Resistance** – Draw horizontal lines at recent lows/highs.  
3. **Examine Candlesticks** – Look for bullish patterns (e.g., hammer, bullish engulfing) forming near support.  
4. **Check Moving Averages**  
   - Is the price above the 20‑day SMA?  
   - Is there a golden cross forming?  
5. **Read Momentum Indicators**  
   - Is RSI < 30 (oversold) or > 70 (overbought)?  
   - Has MACD just crossed above its signal line?  
6. **Confirm with Volume** (optional but recommended) – Higher-than‑average volume on the bullish candle adds credibility.  
7. **Set Trade Parameters**  
   - **Entry:** Near the identified support level after a confirming candle.  
   - **Stop‑loss:** Slightly below the support zone (e.g., 1‑2 % lower).  
   - **Target:** Just below the next resistance level or a fixed risk‑reward ratio (e.g., 1:2).  

### 5.2 Sample Trade on RIL

| Step | Observation | Decision |
|------|-------------|----------|
| **Support** | ₹2,200–₹2,220 zone tested 3× in 30 days | Treat as entry area |
| **Candlestick** | 19 May: Bullish engulfing, close at ₹2,250 | Positive entry signal |
| **MA** | Price > 20‑day SMA (₹2,250) but < 50‑day SMA (₹2,300) | Short‑term uptrend, long‑term neutral |
| **RSI** | 14‑day RSI = 32 (near oversold) | Supports bounce expectation |
| **MACD** | MACD line crossed above signal line on 18 May | Momentum turning bullish |
| **Volume** | Volume 1.4× average on 19 May | Confirmation |
| **Trade** | **Buy** at ₹2,255; **Stop‑loss** at ₹2,190; **Target** at ₹2,340 (near next resistance) | Risk‑reward ≈ 1:2.5 |

If the price respects the support and moves upward, Rohit has a statistically sound entry based purely on chart information, complementing the fundamental view that RIL’s earnings remain strong (as discussed in the earlier *Fundamental Analysis* chapter).

---

## 6. Common Pitfalls for Beginners and How to Avoid Them

| Pitfall | Why It Happens | Simple Fix |
|---------|----------------|------------|
| **Over‑reliance on a single indicator** | A lone signal can be a false alarm. | Use **multiple confirmations** (e.g., candlestick + support + RSI). |
| **Ignoring the market context** | Technical patterns differ in trending vs. ranging markets. | First assess the **overall trend** with moving averages before applying patterns. |
| **Setting stops too tight** | Small price wiggles trigger stop‑losses prematurely. | Place stops **just beyond** support/resistance, allowing normal volatility. |
| **Chasing the price** | Buying after a big move often leads to buying at the top. | Stick to **pre‑defined entry rules**; avoid emotional decisions. |
| **Forgetting the “big picture”** | Focusing only on charts can ignore fundamental shifts (e.g., earnings surprise). | Combine technical analysis with the **fundamental insights** already covered. |

---

## 7. Quick Reference Cheat Sheet

| Tool | What It Shows | Typical Use |
|------|---------------|-------------|
| **Candlestick patterns** | Price action within a period | Spot reversal or continuation signals |
| **Support / Resistance** | Historical price levels where buying/selling re‑emerges | Entry, exit, stop‑loss placement |
| **Moving Averages (SMA/EMA)** | Smoothed price trend | Trend direction, dynamic support/resistance |
| **RSI** | Momentum on a 0‑100 scale | Overbought/oversold conditions |
| **MACD** | Relationship between two EMAs | Trend strength and direction changes |

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Candlesticks** condense open, high, low, and close into a single visual; bullish and bearish patterns near support/resistance are strong entry signals.  
- **Support** acts as a price floor, **resistance** as a ceiling; drawing these zones provides natural entry and exit points.  
- **Moving averages** smooth price noise; crossovers (golden/death) and price‑relative positions reveal trend direction.  
- **RSI** identifies overbought (> 70) or oversold (< 30) conditions, while **MACD** captures momentum shifts through line crossovers and histogram changes.  
- A **systematic workflow**—checking support, candlesticks, moving averages, and momentum indicators—helps beginners like Rohit make disciplined, data‑driven trade decisions.  

By mastering these basics, you now have a practical toolbox to read Indian stock charts, spot entry opportunities, and protect yourself from common trading traps. The next step will be to integrate these technical insights with the portfolio‑building principles covered later in the book. Happy charting!

modules.title: Portfolio Construction & Risk Management
modules.content:
## Why Diversification Matters – A Real‑World Snapshot  

Imagine you bought shares of a single mid‑cap company that you liked because its product seemed promising. In the first month the stock jumped 25 %, and you thought you’d struck gold. The next month, the company missed earnings, the regulator issued a notice, and the share price slumped 40 %. Your entire ₹2 lakh investment is now worth only ₹1.2 lakh.  

Now picture the same ₹2 lakh spread across 10 different stocks from various sectors—large‑cap banks, a pharma leader, a technology firm, a metal‑producer, a renewable‑energy company, plus a gold ETF and a debt fund. Even if a few of those holdings suffer large losses, the gains from the others can cushion the blow, often leaving your overall portfolio value much closer to the original amount.  

That protective effect is **diversification**. It is the cornerstone of portfolio construction and the first line of defence against the inevitable ups and downs of the Indian stock market.

---

## 1. Building a Diversified Portfolio  

### 1.1 What Is Diversification?  

Diversification means **spreading your investment across a range of assets that do not move exactly together**. When one investment underperforms, another may outperform, reducing the overall volatility of your portfolio.

### 1.2 How to Diversify in the Indian Context  

| Asset Class | Typical Instruments | Role in a Portfolio |
|-------------|--------------------|---------------------|
| **Equities** | Large‑cap (e.g., HDFC Bank), Mid‑cap, Small‑cap stocks, Sectoral ETFs | Growth engine; higher expected returns, higher volatility |
| **Debt** | Government bonds, Corporate bonds, Liquid mutual funds, Fixed‑maturity plans (FMPs) | Income and stability; lower volatility |
| **Gold** | Gold ETFs (e.g., Gold ETF‑30), Sovereign Gold Bonds | Hedge against inflation and currency risk |
| **Real Estate** | REITs (e.g., Embassy Office Parks REIT) | Income and diversification beyond traditional equity‑debt mix |
| **Cash / Short‑term Instruments** | Savings account, Treasury bills | Liquidity for emergencies and opportunistic buying |

A simple starter mix for a beginner with ₹2 lakh could look like:

* 60 % equities (large‑cap + a small‑cap blend)  
* 20 % debt (liquid fund + short‑term bond fund)  
* 10 % gold (Gold ETF)  
* 10 % cash (for flexibility)

### 1.3 Practical Steps to Diversify  

1. **List the asset classes** you want exposure to (see table above).  
2. **Choose a few representative securities** in each class—preferably those you have already evaluated using the tools from *Fundamental Analysis: Evaluating Companies* and *Technical Analysis Basics*.  
3. **Allocate capital** to each security so that the weight of any single holding does not dominate the portfolio (a common rule of thumb is ≤ 10 % per stock for beginners).  
4. **Monitor overlap**—if two stocks belong to the same sector, their price movements may be highly correlated, reducing the benefit of diversification.  

---

## 2. Setting Asset Allocation Based on Your Risk Tolerance  

### 2.1 Understanding Risk Tolerance  

Your **risk tolerance** is the amount of volatility you are comfortable experiencing in pursuit of higher returns. It depends on:

* **Financial goals** (e.g., buying a home in 5 years vs. retirement in 30 years)  
* **Income stability** (salaried employee vs. business owner)  
* **Emotional comfort** with market swings  

### 2.2 A Simple Risk‑Tolerance Questionnaire  

| Question | Low‑Risk Answer | Medium‑Risk Answer | High‑Risk Answer |
|----------|----------------|--------------------|-----------------|
| If your portfolio fell 15 % in a month, what would you do? | Sell to limit loss | Hold and review fundamentals | Hold and possibly buy more |
| What is your investment horizon? | ≤ 3 years | 4‑10 years | > 10 years |
| How much of your total savings are you willing to invest in equities? | ≤ 30 % | 31‑60 % | > 60 % |

Count the number of “Low”, “Medium”, and “High” answers to gauge your tolerance:

* **Conservative** – mostly Low answers  
* **Moderate** – mix of Low and Medium  
* **Aggressive** – mostly High answers  

### 2.3 Translating Tolerance into Asset Allocation  

| Risk Profile | Suggested Allocation (Equities : Debt : Gold : Cash) |
|--------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| **Conservative** | 30 % : 55 % : 10 % : 5 % |
| **Moderate** | 55 % : 30 % : 10 % : 5 % |
| **Aggressive** | 80 % : 10 % : 5 % : 5 % |

> **Note:** These percentages are starting points. Adjust them based on personal circumstances and market outlook.

### 2.4 Example Allocation for a Moderate Investor  

Assume a ₹2 lakh portfolio, moderate risk:

| Asset Class | % of Portfolio | Amount (₹) | Example Instruments |
|-------------|----------------|------------|---------------------|
| Equities | 55 % | 1,10,000 | HDFC Bank, Infosys, Reliance Industries, a Mid‑cap ETF |
| Debt | 30 % | 60,000 | Liquid fund (e.g., ICICI Prudential Liquid Fund), 1‑year FMP |
| Gold | 10 % | 20,000 | Gold ETF‑30 |
| Cash | 5 % | 10,000 | Savings account, for opportunistic buying |

---

## 3. Measuring Portfolio Risk – Variance & Standard Deviation  

### 3.1 The Intuition Behind Variance and Standard Deviation  

* **Variance** tells you how far the returns of an asset (or portfolio) deviate from their average over a period.  
* **Standard deviation** is simply the square‑root of variance; it is expressed in the same units as returns (percentage), making it easier to interpret.  

A higher standard deviation → higher volatility → higher risk.

### 3.2 Calculating the Risk of a Two‑Asset Portfolio  

Suppose you hold:

| Asset | Weight (w) | Annualized Return (µ) | Standard Deviation (σ) |
|-------|------------|-----------------------|------------------------|
| Stock A (large‑cap) | 0.6 | 12 % | 18 % |
| Debt Fund B | 0.4 | 7 % | 5 % |
| **Correlation (ρ)** between A and B | — | — | 0.2 |

The portfolio’s variance (σ²ₚ) is:

\[
\sigma^2_p = w_A^2 \sigma_A^2 + w_B^2 \sigma_B^2 + 2 w_A w_B \sigma_A \sigma_B \rho_{AB}
\]

Plugging the numbers:

* \(w_A^2 \sigma_A^2 = 0.6^2 \times 0.18^2 = 0.011664\)  
* \(w_B^2 \sigma_B^2 = 0.4^2 \times 0.05^2 = 0.0004\)  
* \(2 w_A w_B \sigma_A \sigma_B \rho = 2 \times 0.6 \times 0.4 \times 0.18 \times 0.05 \times 0.2 = 0.001728\)

\[
\sigma^2_p = 0.011664 + 0.0004 + 0.001728 = 0.013792
\]

Standard deviation:

\[
\sigma_p = \sqrt{0.013792} \approx 11.7\%
\]

**Interpretation:** The blended portfolio is expected to fluctuate about ± 11.7 % each year, considerably lower than the 18 % volatility of the equity component alone.

### 3.3 Extending to Multiple Assets  

When you have more than two assets, you build a **variance‑covariance matrix** that captures each asset’s variance and every pair’s covariance (derived from correlation). Spreadsheet software (Excel/Google Sheets) can compute the portfolio variance with the matrix formula:

\[
\sigma^2_p = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{\Sigma} \mathbf{w}
\]

where **w** is the column vector of weights and **Σ** is the covariance matrix.

### 3.4 Quick‑Start Tool for Beginners  

1. **Collect monthly returns** for each holding over the past 12 months (use data from the BSE or NSE websites).  
2. **Calculate the average return and standard deviation** for each security (Excel’s `AVERAGE` and `STDEV.P`).  
3. **Determine pairwise correlations** with `CORREL`.  
4. **Apply the formula** above (or use an online portfolio‑risk calculator) to get the overall standard deviation.  

Even a rough estimate helps you compare two portfolio proposals and choose the one that aligns with your risk tolerance.

---

## 4. Protecting Your Portfolio – Stop‑Loss and Position‑Sizing  

### 4.1 Stop‑Loss Orders – The Safety Net  

A **stop‑loss order** tells your broker to sell a security automatically once its price reaches a pre‑defined level. It limits how much you can lose on a single trade.

* **Fixed‑percentage stop:** Set, for example, a 10 % stop‑loss below the entry price.  
* **Trailing stop:** The stop price moves up as the stock price rises, locking in gains while still protecting against downside.

> **Tip:** In *Setting Up Your Trading Infrastructure* you learned how to place a stop‑loss on BSE Online. The same steps apply to any NSE‑based broker platform.

### 4.2 Position‑Sizing – Controlling How Much You Trade  

Position‑sizing determines **how many shares or units you buy** based on the amount of capital you are willing to risk on that trade.

**Common rule:** Risk no more than 1‑2 % of total capital on any single position.

#### Example with ₹2 lakh Capital  

1. **Decide risk per trade:** 1 % of ₹2 lakh = ₹2,000.  
2. **Select a stock** entering at ₹500 per share.  
3. **Choose a stop‑loss** 8 % below entry → ₹460.  
4. **Calculate risk per share:** ₹500 – ₹460 = ₹40.  
5. **Number of shares you can afford:** ₹2,000 ÷ ₹40 = 50 shares.  

Thus you buy 50 shares (₹25,000 total) and your maximum loss, if the stop triggers, will be roughly ₹2,000.

### 4.3 Combining Stop‑Loss and Position‑Sizing  

| Step | Action |
|------|--------|
| 1 | Define overall risk per trade (e.g., 1 % of portfolio). |
| 2 | Identify entry price and stop‑loss level. |
| 3 | Compute risk per share/unit. |
| 4 | Divide allowed risk by risk per share to get quantity. |
| 5 | Place the trade **and** immediately set the stop‑loss order. |

By following this disciplined process, you avoid the common beginner pitfall of “over‑trading” or “letting losses run”.

---

## 5. Keeping the Portfolio on Track – Rebalancing  

### 5.1 Why Rebalancing Matters  

Over time, market moves will cause some assets to grow faster than others, shifting your original allocation. Without rebalancing, a “moderate” portfolio can inadvertently become “aggressive”, exposing you to more risk than you intended.

### 5.2 When to Rebalance  

* **Time‑based approach:** Review and rebalance semi‑annually or annually.  
* **Threshold‑based approach:** Rebalance whenever an asset class deviates **more than 5‑10 %** from its target weight.

### 5.3 The Rebalancing Process – Step‑by‑Step  

1. **Calculate current weights** of each holding (value of holding ÷ total portfolio value).  
2. **Compare with target weights** from your asset‑allocation plan.  
3. **Identify over‑weighted assets** (those above target) and under‑weighted assets (below target).  
4. **Sell a portion of the over‑weighted assets** and **use the proceeds** to buy under‑weighted assets, keeping transaction costs in mind.  
5. **Update your records** (spreadsheet or portfolio‑tracking app) with the new quantities and weights.

#### Example  

Your moderate portfolio (target 55 % equities, 30 % debt, 10 % gold, 5 % cash) after 9 months looks like:

| Asset | Target % | Current % | Action |
|-------|----------|-----------|--------|
| Equities | 55 % | 68 % | Sell enough to bring to 55 % |
| Debt | 30 % | 22 % | Buy more debt instruments |
| Gold | 10 % | 8 % | Add a small amount of Gold ETF |
| Cash | 5 % | 2 % | Keep a small cash buffer; no immediate action |

If equities have risen to ₹1,36,000 (68 % of ₹2,00,000), you would sell roughly ₹22,000 worth of equities and allocate that amount to debt and gold to restore the intended mix.

### 5.4 Practical Tips for Indian Investors  

* **Use low‑cost index funds or ETFs** for broad exposure; they simplify rebalancing because one fund can represent an entire asset class.  
* **Take advantage of SIP (Systematic Investment Plan) exits** to add to under‑weighted buckets without incurring separate brokerage charges.  
* **Watch tax implications**—while this chapter does not cover taxes, frequent selling can generate short‑term capital gains; balance the need to rebalance with tax efficiency.

---

## 6. Putting It All Together – A Mini‑Case Study  

**Investor Profile:** Riya, 28 years old, ₹2 lakh savings, moderate risk tolerance, 7‑year horizon to buy a house.

### 6.1 Step 1 – Define Asset Allocation  

| Asset | Target % | Amount (₹) |
|-------|----------|------------|
| Equities (large‑cap + mid‑cap) | 55 % | 1,10,000 |
| Debt (liquid fund) | 30 % | 60,000 |
| Gold (Gold ETF‑30) | 10 % | 20,000 |
| Cash | 5 % | 10,000 |

### 6.2 Step 2 – Choose Specific Securities  

* **Equities:** 40 % HDFC Bank, 15 % Infosys, 10 % a Mid‑cap ETF (e.g., Nifty Midcap 150 ETF).  
* **Debt:** ICICI Prudential Liquid Fund.  
* **Gold:** Gold ETF‑30.  

### 6.3 Step 3 – Apply Position‑Sizing & Stop‑Loss  

For HDFC Bank entry at ₹1,600:

* Risk per trade = 1 % of portfolio = ₹2,000.  
* Desired stop‑loss = 8 % → ₹1,472.  
* Risk per share = ₹128.  
* Shares to buy = ₹2,000 ÷ ₹128 ≈ 15 shares (₹24,000).  

Set a stop‑loss order at ₹1,472 immediately after purchase.

### 6.4 Step 4 – Estimate Portfolio Risk  

Using past 12‑month monthly returns, Riya calculates:

* Equity basket σ ≈ 18 %  
* Debt fund σ ≈ 4 %  
* Gold σ ≈ 12 %  
* Correlations: equity‑debt 0.25, equity‑gold 0.30, debt‑gold 0.10  

Plugging into the covariance matrix, the overall portfolio standard deviation comes out to **≈ 11 %**, matching her moderate‑risk target.

### 6.5 Step 5 – Rebalance After One Year  

After 12 months, equities have risen to 70 % of the portfolio. Riya sells ₹12,000 worth of HDFC Bank and reallocates it to the debt fund and gold ETF, bringing the weights back to the original targets.

---

## Key Takeaways  

* **Diversification** reduces portfolio volatility by spreading investments across uncorrelated assets.  
* **Asset allocation** should reflect your personal risk tolerance; a simple questionnaire can guide you toward a conservative, moderate, or aggressive mix.  
* **Portfolio risk** can be quantified with variance and standard deviation; a basic two‑asset formula already shows the benefit of mixing equities with debt.  
* **Stop‑loss orders** and **position‑sizing** are practical tools that limit individual trade losses and preserve capital; aim to risk no more than 1–2 % of your total portfolio on any single position.  
* **Regular rebalancing** (time‑based or threshold‑based) restores your intended allocation, preventing drift into unintended risk levels.  

By integrating these principles—diversification, calibrated allocation, risk measurement, disciplined trade execution, and periodic rebalancing—you lay a solid foundation for a resilient, growth‑oriented investment journey in the Indian stock market.

## A Real‑World Walk‑through: Riya’s First Trade  

Riya, a 28‑year‑old software engineer from Bengaluru, has just finished reading the earlier chapters on market fundamentals and portfolio construction. She has **₹2 lakh** saved in a fixed deposit and wants to use a part of it to buy shares of a well‑known listed company. This section shows, step‑by‑step, how she moves from logging into her broker’s trading platform to seeing the trade reflected in her portfolio, and what she must do next to stay tax‑compliant.

---

## 1. From Login to Order Execution  

| Step | What Riya Does | What Happens Behind the Scenes |
|------|----------------|--------------------------------|
| 1. **Open the trading app** | Launches the **BSE Online** mobile app (or web portal). | The app connects to the broker’s order‑management system (OMS). |
| 2. **Authenticate** | Enters her **username**, **password**, and the OTP sent to her phone (two‑factor authentication). | The broker verifies her credentials and confirms the session is secure. |
| 3. **Select the stock** | Types “INFY” in the search bar, sees the latest **market price** and volume. | Real‑time price feed from the exchange is displayed. |
| 4. **Decide quantity** | Chooses to buy **200 shares** (₹2 lakh ÷ current price ≈ ₹150 per share). | The platform checks her **demat** account balance and **margin** (if using leverage). |
| 5. **Pick an order type** | Selects **Limit Order** at ₹148.50, meaning the trade will execute only at that price or better. | The OMS records the order and places it in the **order book** of the exchange. |
| 6. **Review & confirm** | Clicks **‘Buy’**, sees a summary: 200 × ₹148.50 = ₹29,700 + brokerage + GST + STT. | The broker calculates **transaction charges** (brokerage, securities transaction tax – STT, GST, clearing‑house fees). |
| 7. **Order acknowledgment** | Receives an **order ID** and a “Pending” status. | The exchange matches the order when a seller is found at the limit price. |
| 8. **Execution** | Within seconds, the order is **filled**; Riya sees a “Completed” status and a trade confirmation. | The trade is settled through the **clearing corporation**; shares move to Riya’s **demat** account. |
| 9. **Post‑trade receipt** | Downloads the **trade confirmation PDF** for her records. | The broker posts the transaction to the **account statement** and updates the portfolio view. |

> **Tip for beginners:** Always double‑check the **total cost** (price × quantity + charges) before confirming the order. Small fees can add up, especially on frequent trades.

---

## 2. Monitoring and Reviewing Portfolio Performance  

### 2.1. The Dashboard  

After the trade, Riya’s **portfolio dashboard** shows:

- **Current holdings:** 200 INFY shares, cost basis ₹29,700.  
- **Unrealized P&L:** Difference between the current market price and cost basis.  
- **Realized P&L:** Zero at this point (no shares sold yet).  
- **Cash balance:** Remaining ₹1,70,300 (plus any unsettled funds).

### 2.2. Key Metrics to Watch  

- **Day‑to‑day change** (percentage and rupee amount).  
- **Portfolio‑level exposure** (e.g., % of total capital in equities).  
- **Sector concentration** (how many shares belong to the same industry).  

These metrics help Riya stay aligned with the **risk management** principles discussed in Chapter 8.

### 2 .3. Periodic Review Routine  

| Frequency | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| **Daily** | Check market price, update alerts for price targets or stop‑loss levels. |
| **Weekly** | Review **unrealized gains/losses**; decide if any position needs trimming. |
| **Quarterly** | Re‑balance the portfolio to maintain the asset allocation set in Chapter 8. |
| **Year‑end** | Export the **annual statement** for tax filing; verify cost basis with broker’s records. |

Most brokers let you **export statements** in CSV or PDF format, making the next section—tax calculation—much easier.

---

## 3. Calculating Capital Gains Tax  

### 3.1. Short‑Term vs. Long‑Term  

- **Short‑Term Capital Gains (STCG):** Profit on shares held **≤ 12 months**. Taxed at **15 %** (plus applicable surcharge and cess).  
- **Long‑Term Capital Gains (LTCG):** Profit on shares held **> 12 months**. Taxed at **10 %** on gains **exceeding ₹1 lakh** in a financial year (no indexation benefit).  

> **Note:** The **holding period** starts from the **trade settlement date**, not the order date.

### 3.2. Sample Calculation  

Riya sells 100 INFY shares on 15 Oct 2025 at ₹170 each.

| Item | Amount |
|------|--------|
| **Sale proceeds** | 100 × ₹170 = **₹17,000** |
| **Cost basis** (average price from purchase) | 100 × ₹148.50 = **₹14,850** |
| **Gross profit** | **₹2,150** |
| **Holding period** | 5 months → **STCG** |
| **Tax rate** | 15 % |
| **STCG tax** | 0.15 × ₹2,150 = **₹322.50** |
| **Net amount received** | ₹17,000 − ₹322.50 = **₹16,677.50** |

If Riya had held the shares for 14 months, the same ₹2,150 profit would be **LTCG**. Since the profit is below the ₹1 lakh exemption, **no tax** would be payable.

### 3.3. Using Broker Statements  

- **Cost basis column:** Shows the average purchase price per share (including brokerage).  
- **Realized gains column:** Summarises profit/loss for each sale.  
- **Form 26AS:** The Income Tax Department’s consolidated tax statement; match the broker‑reported gains with the entries here.

---

## 4. Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) on Securities Transactions  

### 4.1. When Does TDS Apply?  

- **Sale of securities (shares, debentures, units) where the **gross sale consideration exceeds ₹50 lakh** in a financial year.  
- **Derivative transactions** (futures/options) when the **gross turnover** exceeds ₹10 lakh.  

The **TDS rate** is **0.1 %** of the sale consideration (or turnover) and is deducted **at the time of settlement** by the broker.

### 4.2. Practical Example  

Suppose Riya’s total sales in FY 2025‑26 amount to **₹55 lakh**. The broker will:

1. **Deduct TDS:** 0.1 % × ₹55 lakh = **₹5,500**.  
2. **Deposit the amount** with the Income Tax Department and issue a **TDS certificate (Form 16A)**.  

Riya can claim this **₹5,500** as a **tax credit** while filing her income tax return. If her actual tax liability on capital gains is lower, the excess TDS is refunded.

### 4.3. Points to Remember  

- **PAN must be linked** to the trading account; otherwise, TDS is deducted at **higher rates** (up to 5 %).  
- **TDS is not a final tax**—it is merely a pre‑payment. The final tax is computed on the net capital gains after all deductions.  
- The **TDS certificate** appears in **Form 26AS**; reconcile it with your broker’s statements.

---

## 5. Staying Compliant with SEBI Regulations  

### 5.1. Core Compliance Requirements  

| Requirement | What It Means for Riya |
|-------------|------------------------|
| **KYC (Know Your Customer)** | Submit PAN, Aadhaar, and address proof to the broker; updates must be done annually. |
| **Demat account** | Holds the actual shares; mandatory for all equity‑linked trades. |
| **SEBI‑registered broker** | Ensures trades are executed on a **regulated exchange** and that her funds are safe. |
| **Periodic reporting** | Brokers report all trades to the **clearing corporation** and to the **Income Tax Department** (via Form 26AS). |
| **Beneficial ownership disclosure** | If holdings cross **5 %** of a listed company’s equity, Riya (or the entity she acts for) must file a **Form 24** with the exchange. |
| **Insider trading rules** | No trading on the basis of unpublished price‑sensitive information; violation can lead to severe penalties. |
| **Margin & leverage limits** | SEBI caps margin requirements; brokers must disclose the **margin call** and **liquidation** processes. |

### 5.2. Record‑Keeping Checklist  

- **Trade confirmations** (PDFs) for every buy/sell.  
- **Broker statements** (monthly/annual).  
- **Form 16A** (TDS certificates) and **Form 26AS** (tax credit statements).  
- **Demat account statements** (showing share holdings).  
- **Portfolio performance reports** (for personal tracking and tax filing).  

Keeping these documents organized (e.g., in a dedicated folder on cloud storage) simplifies the annual **income‑tax return** filing and helps during any audit.

### 5.3. Filing the Income Tax Return  

1. **Gather** all broker statements, TDS certificates, and Form 26AS.  
2. **Calculate** net STCG and LTCG (as shown in Section 3).  
3. **Enter** the figures in the appropriate I‑Tax schedule (Schedule CG).  
4. **Claim** TDS credit (₹5,500 in the example) under **‘Tax deducted at source’**.  
5. **Pay** any additional tax liability before the due date (usually 31 July for FY 2025‑26).  

Most brokerage firms now provide a **‘Tax Summary’** export that directly maps to the I‑Tax schedules, reducing manual entry errors.

---

## 6. Practical Compliance Checklist – After Every Trade  

1. **Verify trade confirmation** – ensure quantity, price, and charges match your order.  
2. **Update portfolio dashboard** – note realized/unrealized gains.  
3. **Save the PDF** in a dated folder (e.g., “2025‑Q3 Trades”).  
4. **Check for TDS** – if the cumulative sales cross ₹50 lakh, confirm TDS deduction and receipt.  
5. **Re‑assess risk exposure** – does the new position keep you within the asset‑allocation limits set in Chapter 8?  
6. **Set alerts** – price targets, stop‑loss, or dividend dates.  
7. **Monthly reconciliation** – match broker statements with your own records and with Form 26AS.  

Following this routine keeps Riya’s investing disciplined, tax‑efficient, and fully compliant with SEBI regulations.

---

## ## Key Takeaways  

- **Step‑by‑step execution**: From login to order confirmation, every action is logged and settled through the exchange’s clearing system.  
- **Portfolio monitoring**: Use the broker’s dashboard to track unrealized/realized P&L, set alerts, and conduct periodic reviews aligned with risk‑management goals.  
- **Capital gains tax**: STCG (≤ 12 months) taxed at 15 %; LTCG (> 12 months) taxed at 10 % on gains above ₹1 lakh. Calculate tax using the broker’s cost‑basis and sale price.  
- **TDS on large transactions**: 0.1 % is deducted when yearly sales exceed ₹50 lakh; the amount is creditable against final tax liability.  
- **SEBI compliance**: Maintain up‑to‑date KYC, demat, and record‑keeping; disclose holdings > 5 % and avoid insider trading.  
- **Check‑list habit**: After each trade, confirm the trade slip, update the portfolio, verify TDS, reassess risk, and store documents for tax filing.  

By mastering the workflow of placing trades, tracking performance, and meeting tax and regulatory obligations, beginners like Riya can transition from learning the basics to becoming confident, compliant investors in the Indian stock market.

# Chapter 1: Understanding the Indian Stock Market Landscape

## The Stock Market in One Minute: A Real‑World Glimpse  

Imagine Rahul, a 25‑year‑old software engineer in Bengaluru. He has saved **₹2 lakh** from his salary and hears his friends brag about turning a modest amount into a sizable corpus by “buying stocks.” Rahul wonders:

- **Where do stocks actually trade?**  
- **Who decides the price of a share?**  
- **Is there a watchdog ensuring the market is fair?**  

In the next few pages you will see how Rahul’s questions are answered by the structure of the Indian stock market, the exchanges that host the trade, the regulator that keeps the system honest, the players who make every transaction possible, and the rhythm of market cycles that every investor eventually learns to read.

---

## 1. What Is a Stock Market and Why Does It Exist?  

A **stock market** is a **organized platform** where **ownership units**—called **shares**—of publicly listed companies are bought and sold. It serves three core purposes:

1. **Capital Formation**  
   Companies raise money by issuing shares to the public (the *primary market*). The funds can be used for expansion, research, debt repayment, or any corporate need.  

2. **Price Discovery**  
   The market aggregates the opinions of thousands of buyers and sellers, translating them into a **market price** for each share. This price reflects collective expectations about a company’s future earnings, risk, and growth prospects.  

3. **Liquidity**  
   Investors can convert their shares into cash quickly because there is a continuous flow of buyers and sellers. Liquidity reduces the cost of entering or exiting an investment position.  

In simple terms, the stock market is **the country’s giant, transparent auction house** where capital meets opportunity.

---

## 2. The Two Pillars of Indian Trading: NSE and BSE  

India’s equity trading is dominated by two exchanges that operate side by side, each with its own history, technology, and benchmark index.

### 2.1 Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE)  

| Feature | Details |
|---|---|
| **Founded** | 1875 – Asia’s oldest stock exchange |
| **Trading Platform** | **BSE Online** (formerly BOLT) |
| **Benchmark Index** | **SENSEX** (30‑stock index) |
| **Listed Companies** | > 5,000 (as of 2024) |
| **Unique Trait** | First Indian exchange to launch a **dematerialised (demat) system** in 1996, simplifying share transfer. |

The BSE’s long heritage makes it a cultural landmark; many Indian families recall the iconic **“BSE building”** as a symbol of financial ambition.

### 2.2 National Stock Exchange (NSE)  

| Feature | Details |
|---|---|
| **Founded** | 1992 – created to bring electronic trading to India |
| **Trading Platform** | **NSE Trade‑Now** (full‑electronic order‑matching) |
| **Benchmark Index** | **NIFTY 50** (50‑stock index) |
| **Listed Companies** | > 3,000 (as of 2024) |
| **Unique Trait** | First Indian exchange to adopt a **fully automated screen‑based system**, eliminating the old “floor‑trading” model. |

Because of its speed, transparency, and deep liquidity, the NSE processes **≈ 90 % of equity‑trading volume** in India today.  

### 2.3 Quick Comparison  

- **Age:** BSE (1875) vs. NSE (1992)  
- **Technology:** BSE – hybrid (electronic + legacy), NSE – fully electronic  
- **Liquidity:** NSE generally higher, especially for large‑cap stocks  
- **Indices:** SENSEX (30 stocks) vs. NIFTY 50 (50 stocks)  

Both exchanges **share the same regulatory framework** and **inter‑operate** through the **National Securities Clearing Corporation Limited (NSCCL)** for settlement, ensuring that a trade executed on either venue settles the same way.

---

## 3. SEBI – The Guardian of Fair Play  

### 3.1 Who Is SEBI?  

The **Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)** is the **statutory regulator** for the securities market, established in 1992 under the **SEBI Act, 1992**. Its mission can be summed up as:

- **Protecting investors** (especially retail participants) from fraud and malpractice.  
- **Regulating market intermediaries** (brokers, depositories, rating agencies).  
- **Developing the securities market** through policy, innovation, and infrastructure upgrades.  

### 3.2 Core Functions  

| Function | Typical Activity |
|---|---|
| **Registration & Licensing** | Grants licences to brokers, mutual funds, and other market participants. |
| **Listing Standards** | Sets **eligibility criteria** for companies that wish to list on NSE/BSE (e.g., minimum net worth, profitability, corporate governance). |
| **Surveillance & Enforcement** | Monitors trading patterns for **insider trading**, **price manipulation**, and **unfair practices**; imposes penalties or bans. |
| **Investor Education** | Runs campaigns (e.g., **“Investing for All”**) and publishes guidelines on how to avoid scams. |
| **Market Development** | Introduces new products (e.g., **exchange‑traded funds – ETFs**) and upgrades settlement cycles (currently **T+2**, meaning settlement occurs two business days after trade). |

### 3.3 How SEBI Keeps the Market Clean  

1. **Real‑time Market Surveillance** – SEBI’s **Market Surveillance System (MSS)** scans every order flow for abnormal spikes.  
2. **Insider‑Trading Rules** – Company insiders must disclose any share transactions within **two trading days**; failure can lead to hefty fines.  
3. **Regulatory Filings** – Listed companies file quarterly and annual reports on **MoneyControl** or **BSE/NSE websites**, ensuring transparency.  

A recent (2023) SEBI crackdown on **“pump‑and‑dump” schemes** on social media platforms illustrates that the regulator actively pursues illicit practices, reinforcing investor confidence.
